facts.text: The theoretical framework in which a country decides its friends, its bloc and its position in international relations is called foreign policy.
facts.quote: Each country has to decide the nations with which it should be friendly, in which bloc it should participate or what position it should take in international relations. ... The theoretical framework in which such decisions are taken is called foreign policy.

facts.text: Every sovereign and independent country decides its own foreign policy.
facts.quote: Every sovereign and independent country decides its own foreign policy.

facts.text: National interest means safeguarding independence and sovereignty; it also includes economic development and increasing national power.
facts.quote: National interest implies the means through which the independence and sovereignty of our country can be safeguarded. National interest also includes efforts to achieve our economic development and to take steps towards increasing our national power.

facts.text: Defence, i.e. protection of the country's independence, sovereignty and integrity, is the highest national interest.
facts.quote: Defence, i.e. the protection of our country's independence, sovereignty and integrity is the highest national interest.

facts.text: Economic development is an important national interest, next only to defence; an economically weak nation cannot maintain its independence.
facts.quote: An economically weak nation will not be able to maintain its independence. Hence economic development is understood to be an important national interest, next only to defence.

facts.text: National interest is the goal and foreign policy is the means to achieve it.
facts.quote: National interest is considered to be the goal and foreign policy is considered to be the means to achieve it.

facts.text: Goals of nations change with conditions and time, so national interest changes; therefore foreign policy is always dynamic.
facts.quote: Goals of nations change with changes in conditions and time. Accordingly, national interest also changes. These changes are reflected in the foreign policy. Therefore, foreign policy is always dynamic.

facts.text: India's foreign policy is based on values like international peace, human rights and security.
facts.quote: For example, India's foreign policy is based on values like international peace, human rights and security.

facts.text: Geographical location as a factor: size, population, topography, coastline and natural resources must be considered in foreign policy.
facts.quote: In sum, the size, population, topography, coastline, availability of natural resources, all these factors need to be considered while deciding the foreign policy of any country.

facts.text: In a democratic political system, the nation's parliament plays a major role in evolving foreign policy; the opposition parties try to regulate it by raising questions.
facts.quote: In a democratic political system, the nation's parliament plays a major role in evolving foreign policy. When different aspects come up for discussion in parliament, the opposition parties try to regulate the foreign policy by raising questions about the same.

facts.text: Federal systems consider constituent States: events in Sri Lanka may affect Tamil Nadu, and events in Bangladesh may affect West Bengal and the North-east Indian States.
facts.quote: For example, events in Sri Lanka may affect Tamil Nadu and those in Bangladesh may affect West Bengal and the North-east Indian States.

facts.text: The economy affects foreign policy in two ways: economic relations, import-export and world trade; and economic security, which is as important as national security. Countries with a strong economy are less dependent on others.
facts.quote: As a result, the economy impacts foreign policy in two ways ... In today's world, the issues of economic security are as important as national security. ... Countries having a strong economy are less dependent on others and they can have an independent foreign policy as well.

facts.text: Political leadership: the President, Prime Minister, Foreign Minister, Defence Minister, Finance Minister and Home Minister have a role in deciding foreign policy.
facts.quote: The President, the Prime Minister, the Foreign Minister, the Defence Minister, the Finance Minister and the Home Minister have a role in deciding foreign policy.

facts.text: Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru contributed the policy of non-alignment to India's foreign policy.
facts.quote: Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru contributed the policy of non-alignment to India's foreign policy.

facts.text: Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee contributed a great deal to improving Sino-Indian relations.
facts.quote: Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee contributed a great deal to improving Sino-Indian relations.

facts.text: Lal Bahadur Shastri's contribution: the Tashkent Agreement.
facts.quote: For example, Lal Bahadur Shastri : Tashkent Agreement

facts.text: Administrative factors: Ministry of External Affairs, Foreign Secretary, Embassies, Diplomatic officers; final decisions are taken by the Prime Minister and the Minister for External Affairs; the National Security Advisor also helps.
facts.quote: Ministry of External Affairs, Foreign Secretary, Embassies in different countries, Diplomatic officers, etc. are the administrative factors ... the final decisions about foreign policy are taken by the Prime Minister and the Minister for External Affairs ... The National Security Advisor also completes this task.

facts.text: India got independence in 1947 and from then started shaping its foreign policy independently.
facts.quote: India got independence in 1947 and from then onwards we started shaping our foreign policy independently.

facts.text: Art. 51 among the Directive Principles of State Policy lays down the broad framework for foreign policy: priority to international peace and security and peaceful resolution of disputes.
facts.quote: Art. 51 among the Directive Principles of State Policy lay down the broad framework for foreign policy. According to it, India should give priority to safeguard international peace and security, and resolve our international problems and disputes by peaceful means.

facts.text: Art. 51: promote international peace and security; maintain just and honourable relations; foster respect for international law and treaty obligations; encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration.
facts.quote: Promote international peace and security. Maintain just and honourable relations between nations. Foster respect for international law and treaty obligations ... Encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.

facts.text: Objectives: defence and boundaries not compromised, unity and integrity, protecting Indian citizens abroad (done by Indian embassies), and economic and commercial relations.
facts.quote: Protect the interests of India's citizens living in other countries. This responsibility is fulfilled by the Indian embassies there.

facts.text: Prime Minister Pandit Nehru shaped India's early foreign policy; he opposed colonialism, took an internationalist position and gave priority to global peace and security.
facts.quote: Prime Minister Pandit Nehru shaped India's foreign policy in the early period. He opposed colonialism through India's foreign policy. He took an internationalist position and gave priority to global peace and security.

facts.text: Early-phase influences: understanding world events independently (peace always central), threats from China and Pakistan, and insistence on self-reliance.
facts.quote: (1) We made an effort to understand all international events and developments independently ... Peace has always been a central feature of India's foreign policy. (2) The threats from China and Pakistan were also taken into account. (3) ... the insistence on self-reliance.

facts.text: India first improved relations with Asia, later Africa; some Asian-African countries joined military pacts led by America or the Soviet Russia, stopping regional development; peace and freedom became the fundamental principles of Non-aligned policy.
facts.quote: But some Asian-African countries participated in the military pacts led either by America or the Soviet Russia. This stopped the process of regional development. ... Peace and freedom became the fundamental principles of Non-aligned policy.

facts.text: Wars happened between India and Pakistan over the Kashmir question in 1947-48 and 1965.
facts.quote: Wars happened between India and Pakistan over the Kashmir question in 1947-48 and 1965.

facts.text: In the third war in 1971, Pakistan broke apart and independent Bangladesh was created.
facts.quote: In the third war, that happened in 1971, Pakistan broke apart and independent Bangladesh was created.

facts.text: In the 1970s India's foreign policy became stable and India rose as a powerful regional power in South Asia.
facts.quote: In the decade of the 1970s, there came about some stability in India's foreign policy. India had risen as a powerful regional power in South Asia.

facts.text: India conducted her first nuclear tests in 1974, proving her nuclear capability.
facts.quote: By conducting nuclear tests in 1974, India had also proved her nuclear capability. ... India conducted her first nuclear tests in 1974.

facts.text: From 1980 changes began: SAARC was established, India started a dialogue with China and interaction with America on security.
facts.quote: From 1980, however, some changes began to take place. In order to increase cooperation among South Asian countries, South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) was established. India initiated a dialogue to improve relations with China. India also started interaction with America for cooperation in the field of security.

facts.text: First stage (1947-1990): with non-alignment India kept friendly relations with all and could get aid from both super powers.
facts.quote: Due to the policy of non-alignment, India could get aid from both the super powers.

facts.text: Defence technology was imported; Soviet Russia, France and Germany helped India.
facts.quote: The technology required for this was imported. Soviet Russia, France and Germany helped India in this matter.

facts.text: First-stage challenges: conflict with Pakistan, creation of Bangladesh and conflict with China.
facts.quote: These included the conflict with Pakistan, creation of Bangladesh and conflict with China.

facts.text: After 1991 India reduced government controls over the economy and adopted the free market policy; trade with neighbours and share in world trade increased.
facts.quote: After 1991, India reduced the government controls over the economy and adopted the free market policy. Naturally, there was an increase in trade with neighbouring countries. Our share in world trade increased.

facts.text: In the second stage, foreign policy became more comprehensive and dynamic, adding economy, trade, education and technology.
facts.quote: India's foreign policy became more comprehensive and dynamic in the second stage. ... Several other dimensions like economy, trade, education and technology got included in foreign policy.

facts.text: In the decade after 1990, relations with Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, etc. became stronger; trade with Israel, Japan, China and the European Union increased.
facts.quote: In the decade after 1990, our relations with the South Asian countries like Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, etc. became stronger. Our trade exchange with Israel, Japan, China and European Union increased.

facts.text: India began to participate more in international and regional organisations, such as G-20 and BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa).
facts.quote: For example, G-20 and BRICS (Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa).

facts.text: Relations with America strengthened, mutual trust grew and India's status rose in the international community.
facts.quote: Our relations with America strengthened. Mutual trust grew. India's status rose in the international community.

facts.text: Immediately after independence India set up the Department of Atomic Energy and the Indian Atomic Energy Commission; its first Chairman was Dr Homi Bhabha.
facts.quote: India undertook the nuclear energy programme immediately after independence. For this we established the Department of Atomic Energy and the Indian Atomic Energy Commission. The first Chairman of the Indian Atomic Energy Commission was Dr Homi Bhabha.

facts.text: Electricity generation was the main purpose of the nuclear programme; it also aimed at military capability.
facts.quote: Even through electricity generation was the main purpose behind the programme, it also aimed at creating military capability.

facts.text: India built nuclear weapons and conducted nuclear tests in 1998.
facts.quote: India built nuclear weapons and conducted nuclear tests in 1998.

facts.text: India accepted the role of a responsible nuclear power and has consistently supported efforts for disarmament.
facts.quote: We have accepted the role of a responsible nuclear power. India has been consistently supporting efforts for disarmament

facts.text: Two treaties were made to stop the spread of nuclear weapons: NNPT and CTBT; India's view is that their conditions benefit big nuclear powers and put unfair restrictions on developing countries.
facts.quote: (1) Nuclear Non Proliferation Treaty (NNPT) (2) Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT). The conditions of both these treaties are of benefit to big nuclear powers and they put unfair restrictions on developing countries
